newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakhstan to privatise major oil producer.
newsitem.headline: Kazakhstan to privatise major oil producer.

text.p: Kazakh Prime Minister Akezhan Kazhegeldin on Thursday said Kazakhstan would sell off its huge Mangistaumunaigaz oil company as part of its wider privatisation plans.
"Six foreign companies are competing in the tender," Kazhegeldin told a news conference in the Kazakh capital Almaty. He did not name any of the companies.
Mangistaumunaigaz, located on the Caspian Sea coast, accounts for around 30 percent of Kazakh oil production.
It produced six million tonnes of oil and 1.8 billion cubic metres of gas in 1995, against total Kazakh oil production of 20.1 million tonnes, according to official figures.

A source at the Kazakh State Privatisation Committee said Kazakhstan's Kazkommertsbank and France's Banque Paribas had been chosen as consultants for the tender, applications for which close on January 15, 1997.
The source said the Kazakh government was also considering placing some of the shares on the London Stock Exchange but gave no details as to what form the listing would take.
"This possibility (London listing) has not been ruled out during the tender process," the source told Reuters.
The Kazakh government, short of cash to pay wages and pensions, has promised to quicken the pace of privatisation and make the process more transparent in order to raise funds.

Grigory Marchenko, an energetic former central banker appointed last month to head the National Securities Commission, has promised to organise sales of stakes in a number of blue-chip companies by May 1997.
But critics say the privatisation process is poorly planned.
Opposition politicians and trade unionists in the resource-rich country of 17 million have accused the government of selling off the republic's mineral wealth too cheaply.
Kazhegeldin defended his government's sales, saying the government was asking fair prices that potential bidders considered fair.
"The public perception absolutely in no way corresponds to the market perception," he said.

He said the government had set a $542 million price tag for a 49 percent stake in state telecoms monopoly NAK Kazakhtelekom, only slightly less than an equivalent price for Russia's Rostelekom, seven times larger than Kazakhtelekom.
Kazhegeldin said corruption was still a problem.
"There is corruption in all states, particularly those undergoing reform," he said. "We must work to decrease corruption here."
